Press Release:


Uncle Kathy: A Carte Blanche Tribute
Described as a humble and fearless leader, anti-Apartheid activist Ahmed Kathrada, who was also affectionately known as “Uncle Kathy”, passed away earlier this week
after battling a short illness. As the country continues to mourn the passing of one of its most revered Liberation heroes, Carte Blanche pays tribute.

Script:


TRIBUTE TO AHMED KATHRADA

V/O: One last journey, one final goodbye. On Wednesday morning thousands gathered to give thanks for the life of a legend.

Thuli: I remember Ahmed Kathrada as everyone’s uncle. A very loving person, a very kind person but a very principled leader.

Derek: A great man of huge humility, hugely modest with a lot of love, a lot of sensitivity, a person who really cares about people.

Goolam: It is a very sad moment for the entire country to lose an icon of this stature, a man that’s irreplaceable, a man that has fought for the people.

V/O: Ahmed Mohamed Kathrada was born in the North-West town of Schweizer-Renecke in 1929, and grew up next door to both Black and White families.

Sahm: He was delivered by an Afrikaner midwife, and he grew up actually speaking Afrikaans, and then because there was no school for Indian children in Schweizer-Reinecke, his father got the African principal to teach him his A, B, Cs. And so, his upbringing was really a non-racial upbringing, and it was only when he got here at the age of 8 in the 1930’s did he see what structural racial segregation was like, and that was the impetus to get him involved in politics.

V/O: Kathrada, or Kathy as he was known, joined the South African Communist party at the age of 12. He was an activist throughout his high school career and mingled with much older comrades, like Wits law student Ismael Meer, at his flat in downtown Johannesburg.

Neeshan: Uncle Kathy looked up to these students who were university students while he was still in high school. When Ismael Meer qualified he then handed over the keys to Kathy. And from the age of 17 or 18 until the time he gets to Rivonia, he then occupies this flat.

V/O: Flat Number 13, Kholvad House became a hub for a generation of activists of all races.

Sophia: We as the younger ones, we also found refuge in Flat 13. Our political education took place at Number 13 Kholvad House.

Mosie: All kinds of people used to come there - Uncle Walter, Uncle Nelson - his flat became known as the people’s flat. Chief Luthuli, at the time of the anti-pass burning, he actually burned his pass in the basin of the flat.

Neeshan: Madiba’s practice, his legal practice moves into this flat when they have to leave Chancellor House. So, for a period of 2 or 3 years, whilst the Treason Trial is going on, he carries out his legal practice from this flat.

V/O: Kathy and his comrades were constantly harassed by the police and spent many months in detention.

Laloo: All together between his trials, political trials, bannings, violations of his banning orders etc, he was arrested 17 different times.

V/O: Laloo Chiba served with Kathy in Umkhonto weSizwe.

Laloo: I first met him in 1954. He has been my brother, my comrade, my friend, my leader, my hero, my political mentor and everything that I hold dear and precious.

V/O: Kathrada and his comrades were forced underground. He adopted a fake identity and became known as Pedro Pereira, and in July 1963 attended a meeting at Liliesleaf Farm outside Johannesburg. He was just 34 years old when the security police raided the farm.

Link: It was in this cottage here at Liliesleaf Farm in Rivonia where Ahmed Kathrada hid, as he and his comrades planned the ill-fated Operation Mayibuye to overthrow the apartheid government. After their arrest they disappeared from public life for more than a quarter of a century.

Laloo: I spent 17, 18 years with Kathy and Madiba and Walter on Robben Island. Kathy looked upon Madiba as his elder brother, Kathy looked upon Walter Sisulu as his own father.

V/O: During the 20 years that Kathy spent on Robben Island, he obtained four degrees through Unisa. In recent years he was awarded five honorary doctorates.

Bongani: What do you think he missed the most in jail?

Laloo: He missed children. The first time he saw and touched a child was after 20 years in prison, can you imagine that?

Neeshan: That for him was the biggest deprivation of jail. And coming out of that he would sit in his flat in the afternoon in Killarney, and just watch the little kids go by.

V/O: In October 1989, after 26 years in prison he was released along with Walter Sisulu and 7 others. Kathrada’s sacrifice had inspired many younger activists to join the struggle, like former Constitutional Court Judge Zak Yacoob.

Zak: He was my political senior when he came out of prison and yet his absolute respectfulness to me, was just about embarrassing actually.

Bongani: What was it like to meet him for the first time?

Zak: It was awesome. I was 43 years old at the time and here was this doyen of a person who had come out of Robben Island. I must say it was an amazing experience to meet him.

V/O: Freedom meant the real work had just begun. Kathy served as Madiba’s parliamentary advisor throughout his Presidency, and shortly afterwards started a Foundation to eradicate racism.

Zak: He believed in equality, he was non-racist, non-sexist in his inner being. Kathy became our neighbor in our flat in Johannesburg about 10 years ago. So my wife and I spent wonderful times with Ahmed and Barbara.

Laloo: When Madiba was released, one of the first things they did was to go to London. And Kathy was on the plane with London, and so was Barbara Hogan, and that is how that relation started.

Neeshan: He called me aside and he said I’m happy that we are alone because I want to say to you here that I love this woman so dearly, and I have come to appreciate all that she has done for me since my release. I said to him you don’t have to tell me that. Please make sure that you tell Barbara that.

Link: Flags have been flying at half-mast around the country as we bid farewell to a great South African leader. His passing has forced us to confront and reflect on the current leadership crisis in the country.

Kgalema: Comrade Kathy took exception to the current culture of feeding frenzy, moral corruption, society of depravity, political dissolution, the dross and sleaze enveloping human mind that would put to shame even some of the vilest political orders known to human history.

V/O: Of all the sentiments expressed at the funeral, it was Kathy’s own words which spoke the loudest. The public letter he wrote to President Zuma resonated strongly when quoted by former President Kgalema Motlanthe.

Kgalema: Comrade Kathy continues: “…and bluntly, if not arrogantly in the face of such persistently widespread criticism, condemnation and demand, is it asking too much to express the hope that you will choose the correct way that is gaining momentum, to consider stepping down?”

Derek: These words made by Comrade Kathy are not uttered lightly. Coming from a man of such great integrity who has given so much to SA, who was held in such high regard by so many South Africans, one has to listen very carefully.

Zweli: We acknowledge that Comrade Kathrada had a right to raise those matters and be forthright, as our leader who has the right to criticize, to guide us and to give us his views.

Thuli: He seemed to feel that people in public office should be ethical people. It’s not enough that they are not criminals. The standard required of them is much higher than that of just not being a criminal.

Magkoba: You God, know the needs of our country and the world. Undertake for us in these times when dark shadows hang over us and over the world; the lamps of decency burn low; raise again prophets in our midst, wise teachers and righteous leaders, so that the people may again find hope for many better tomorrows.

Sahm: He said we mustn’t fixate on individuals; individuals come and go. He would want me to say that he remained a member of the ANC to the last, and he wanted the ANC flag draped over his coffin.

V/O: In the end, both the flag and the coffin fell away, and Kathy’s slim body - wrapped in just the simplest of cloth - was returned to the Earth.

Zak: I will be trying to see what more I can do and I'm hoping more and more people will think like me and say that the best way to remember him, is to take action to make society better, otherwise our praise of Kathy is in vain.
